analysis.one_liner: Phases lead out of paint, plumbing solder, batteries, and packaging, and requires lead inspections of schools and day care centers.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 97–1 on May 25, 1994, but the House never brought it to a vote, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have restricted lead in everyday products: it caps lead in paint, toys, printing inks, and packaging; bans lead solder used in plumbing; sets lead limits for ceramic and crystal food ware; and forces lead-acid batteries into a recycling system with a $10 deposit and retailer take-back. It also requires states receiving federal grants to inspect older schools and day care centers for lead paint and lead dust and to disclose hazards to parents and staff. The Senate passed it with near-unanimous support, but the House never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families, especially children under 7 in older homes, schools, and day care centers, who face the greatest risk of permanent neurologic damage from lead exposure. The bill's own findings state lead poisoning is the most prevalent environmental disease among American children.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in older homes and schools

how_it_helps.text: Bans lead solders commonly used in plumbing and restricts the sale and display of other lead solders, cutting a major source of lead in drinking water.
Caps lead content in paint (0.06 percent), toys, curtain weights, printing inks, and packaging, with phase-ins beginning one to two years after enactment.
Bans landfill disposal and incineration of lead-acid batteries and requires recycling through retailer take-back with a $10 deposit on any new battery not accompanied by a used one.
Requires states receiving federal grants to inspect schools and day care centers built before 1980 for lead paint and lead dust, and to disclose hazards to parents and school staff within 60 days.
Directs the CDC to set standards for blood-lead testing laboratories, and amends food law to treat lead-contaminated packaging, ceramic and crystal ware, and wine as adulterated.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of lead-containing products — solder and plumbing fixture makers, paint producers, packaging and ink makers, and ceramic and crystal ware importers — plus battery retailers, who must accept used batteries and charge deposits. Some compliance costs would be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance timelines run long: packaging lead limits phase down over seven years, plumbing fitting standards could wait five years, and labeling rules up to seven years, leaving exposure routes open while industries adjust.

The final bill is full of carve-outs: industrial and automotive paints are largely exempt, artists' paint is exempt with only a warning label, medical and national-security uses are exempt, and plumbing fittings get a one-year window for an industry voluntary standard before federal rules apply.
A sense-of-the-Senate provision bars the EPA from finalizing any nationwide ban on lead fishing sinkers and lures until alternatives are considered, narrowing the bill's reach on waterfowl risk.

Battery retailers face concrete costs: a not-less-than-$10 deposit on every new battery sold without a used one returned, plus take-back, labeling, and posted-notice duties with fines for noncompliance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside was large: the bill targeted lead, which its findings call the most prevalent environmental disease among American children and a cause of permanent neurologic impairment, and it addressed ongoing sources rather than trying to clean up dispersed lead. The costs — compliance spending by manufacturers and battery retailers, likely passed partly to consumers — were real but modest relative to the health damage from childhood lead exposure. The honest critique is design, not direction: the compromise version stretched timelines to five to seven years, exempted the industrial paint sector, and let plumbing fittings substitute an industry voluntary standard for regulation, so a diluted bill died before its dilution could even take effect.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate 97–1, but the House held it at the desk without ever scheduling a vote, and the bill expired when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Harry Reid introduced the bill on April 1, 1993, and it was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which held subcommittee hearings in June 1993.
The committee reported the bill favorably on October 4, 1993, with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was placed on the Senate calendar.

The Senate took it up by unanimous consent on May 24, 1994, agreed to the committee substitute by voice vote, and passed it the next day by a vote of 97–1, with 54 of 56 Democrats and 43 of 44 Republicans voting yes.
The House received the bill on May 26, 1994, but held it at the desk without referral or a vote; on July 22, 1994, House Resolution 486 returned the papers to the Senate, and the House never acted.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill died without becoming law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lead-using manufacturers — solder, paint, packaging, and ceramic and crystal ware interests — were better off because no new lead restrictions took effect, and House leaders were spared a politically awkward vote on a bill the Senate had passed 97–1. Children in older homes and schools gained nothing, since no federal lead limits or school inspection requirements followed.

for.name: Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 1, 1993, and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Max Baucus
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably to the Senate with a substitute amendment on October 4, 1993, and managed its Senate consideration in May 1994.

for.name: Environmental and public health groups
for.what_they_did: Pushed for federal action on childhood lead poisoning, the issue the bill addressed.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Majority leadership, U.S. House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a vote: the Senate-passed bill sat at the House desk for nearly two months before the papers were returned to the Senate, and the House took no action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Lead product manufacturers and trade associations
against.role: Solder, paint, battery, packaging, and ceramic and crystal ware interests
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against broad lead restrictions and won carve-outs in the final bill: industrial paint exemptions, a voluntary-standard path for plumbing fittings, and a provision blocking a nationwide lead fishing sinker ban.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate vote was near-unanimous across parties: 54 of 56 Democrats and 43 of 44 Republicans voted yes, and the 20 cosponsors included 18 Democrats and 2 Republicans; the bill died in the House without any recorded vote at all.

industries.note: The bill required retailers to take back used batteries, charge at least a $10 deposit, post notices, and label batteries, while manufacturers had to accept used batteries in equal quantities. At the same time, a uniformity clause barred states from enforcing different removability or labeling rules, and mandatory recycling channels locked in the industry's collection role.

industries.industry: Lead solder and plumbing fixture manufacturers
industries.note: Lead plumbing solder — a direct route of lead into drinking water — would be banned, and faucets and fittings would face a leaching standard, though the bill gave the industry a one-year window to write a voluntary standard first.

Lead in paint would be capped at 0.06 percent, though industrial, automotive, agricultural, and lead-chromate paints received long exemptions or substitute-finding processes that could delay restrictions for over a decade.

Intentionally added lead in packaging would be banned after four years, and incidental lead limits would ratchet down to 100 parts per million over seven years, with certificates of compliance required.

industries.industry: Ceramic and crystal ware makers and importers
industries.note: Lead leaching from ceramic and crystal ware into food would be regulated, with noncompliant wares barred from interstate commerce as adulterating food.

Because the bill made recycling the only lawful disposal route and required batteries to flow to smelters, recyclers, retailers, and dismantlers, it guaranteed feedstock to the existing lead recycling channel while keeping batteries out of landfills and incinerators.
